way that some members on this side of the Chamber, including the Minister, went to the
school of hard knocks and the university of life.
To get it down to specifics, in the day that our lovely Minister was on the domestic
purposes benefit, there was no such thing as interest-free loans for students. There was
absolutely no such thing. There were no childcare subsidies in the Minister’s day, and
guess what? Even the accommodation supplement in those days, which had just come
in, was not as good as it is now.
I love it how Labour gets up—I was going to say on its hind legs, but I had better not
say that—and rattles off how bad it is that the Minister has taken away the training
incentive allowance, because she got it and other people will not. Well, I tell members
opposite that when the Minister was on the domestic purposes benefit, she was getting
not a few dollars less but hundreds of dollars less than what a person on the domestic
purposes benefit gets today. If we put it in those words, we see that that is the
disingenuous mode and kōrero from the other side.
I point out that Labour members do not have any experience. Nine years in
Government would have taught them one of two things. Firstly, it would have taught
them that if they were doing a good job, they would have got another 3 years. Like
George Gregan said, I would just love to say that we will have another 3 years and that
side will not, and I will tell the Committee why. It does not matter how sick or under the
weather Chris Carter may be feeling; he was absolutely right.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: So arrogant.

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Oh, no. That has nothing to do with arrogance; it has to do
with listening to the people in the caucus who are thrown out and whom we may not
want to listen to any more. I think that Labour members have not a leg to stand on.
There is no experience. Not one Labour member has any experience.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Oh, really?

items.speaker: Hon TAU HENARE
items.text: Well, at least the Minister knows her way around west
Auckland, and she was not parachuted in without a map. At least she knows where to
go. At least she knows her way around, and she was not parachuted into that electorate.
She won it fair and square.
17 Aug 2010 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 13183

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I want to speak on clause 23, which
concerns advance payment regulations, but before I do, I will address some of the
comments made by Tau Henare. He made claims about people’s lives that were
unjustified and plainly incorrect. I have been on the unemployment benefit and I have
been a sole parent on the domestic purposes benefit. I had the opportunity to receive the
training incentive allowance, and I trained at university so that I would not spend the
rest of my life working at McDonald’s on the minimum wage. As a young woman who
did not have any school qualifications, like many young Māori women of that time, I
had the opportunity to have a tertiary education. Many young Māori women still leave
school without gaining any qualifications, but none the less they have the opportunity to
train in order to get a good qualification, because they have the necessary support and
can therefore get a good job and take care of their family. That is what I did, and that is
what thousands of sole parents do. They use the opportunity to train so that they can do
better for themselves and for their families.
But we would not know that from the rhetoric of the Welfare Working Group—the
very right-wing and very radical anti-beneficiary Welfare Working Group—which
supports faith-based legislation like this bill. The Social Assistance (New Work Tests,
Incentives, and Obligations) Amendment Bill punishes sole parents, and gives a licence
to the community to denigrate sole parents. That is despite the fact that the Minister
herself was a sole parent and understands the circumstances of women like herself and
myself when we were younger and in need of support.
Clause 23 is about the regulations relating to the granting of advance payments of
benefits. This regulation effectively requires some beneficiaries who are considered to
have become too reliant on advances to be compulsorily required, on the advice of their
case manager, to seek budgeting advice. The advance payment of benefits is intended to
meet the immediate needs of beneficiaries, recognising that many beneficiaries will
have exhausted their savings, if indeed they ever had any, because of the low rates of
the main benefit paid.
Since National slashed benefits in the early 1990s—I was working with beneficiaries
at that time and I saw the devastation that that cruelty caused—there has not been a
significant increase in benefits. Benefits are not able to be lived on. They are
insufficient to enable people to care for themselves and for their families. The reliance
on advance payments becomes more acute over time, especially because it becomes
more and more difficult to manage on a meagre income that is insufficient to take care
of basic needs.
This Government, in proposing clause 23, has clearly not learnt from Minister
Maharey in the last Labour Government. Minister Maharey abolished the special
benefit, which was a discretionary benefit and gave an opportunity for case managers to
consider the particular circumstances of the beneficiary who needed extra support. It
was replaced with the regulated temporary additional support allowance, which
removed a level of discretion from the third-tier welfare assistance programme. What
this Government does not understand, and what was unfortunate about Minister
Maharey’s decision, is that we cannot use regulation to deal with the totality of human
experience, especially when we are talking about very low incomes and when people
have ordinary lives that they have to live and simply do not have the income to pay the
power bill, pay the rent, and put decent food on the table.
The discretionary aspect of third-tier assistance is a last resort, because people are
absolutely desperate when they come in for temporary additional support. But when we
take that away, people fall through the cracks. Those people are desperately in need of a
little bit of extra money to cover the very, very basic costs so that their power is not cut
off in the middle of winter, so that they can heat their homes effectively, and so that
13184 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 17 Aug 2010
their kids do not get sick and spend the next 3 weeks off school while they get
medicines and care for them, and cannot do the things that they normally do. This
additional support is just for basic stuff, so that people are able to get through their daily
lives. People fall through the cracks because of the removal of the discretion around
those benefits. They regularly become dependent on food banks, and they get into debt,
perhaps to family members.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: There was a lot of irony in
Tau Henare’s speech this evening, I thought. He berated members opposite for
mentioning the fact that Paula Bennett had been a sole parent beneficiary, but then spent
his entire speech talking about it. The Minister also bemoaned the fact that she had been
brought into the debate, but I have to tell her that she put herself into the debate a long
time ago when she proudly said that she had been a sole parent on a benefit, and that on
that benefit she had managed to get an education and to lift herself up, and that today
she was a Minister of the Crown in the New Zealand Parliament and should be
applauded for that. So I say to the Minister that she brought herself into the debate, and
if it is mentioned by members on this side of the Chamber, then it is because we see it
as an OK thing to do because she did it. Other members, including me, have tonight
talked about their experiences.
Tau Henare said that the Minister came from the school of hard knocks. But I have to
say that she also came from a university education, and we have been saying to
members opposite that if this bill is going to do what National claims, then where is the
plan to get people into work? I want to go into that issue in a moment.
First of all, I want to answer some points made by Hekia Parata. She said in her
speech that there needs to be reciprocity. When the Crown is providing assistance to
those who are on a benefit, then there is some obligation on their part, and I agree with
her. But I ask that member what is magical about the youngest child being 6. I had one
child, and it was a lot easier to be able to do other things when she was 6. But if I had
been a sole parent and had had a 6-year-old, a 7-year-old, a 9-year-old, and an 11-year-
old, the situation would have been totally different. Setting a policy around the youngest
child being 6 does not take account of the other circumstances within that family
situation. That is why it was said in submissions—which the member would have
heard—that if we were to use the policy that exists now within the Ministry of Social
Development, we would have the flexibility to do exactly what this Government wants
to do without actually bringing in legislation.
Members on this side of the Chamber believe that every New Zealander should have
the chance of the Kiwi dream of having a decent job. We want New Zealanders to have
a decent job, with decent pay. But how do we put a person who is on a benefit on that
path? We do not do it by telling them that they have to be work tested when their
youngest child is 6, regardless of the circumstances, and that they need to be able to do
15 hours of work a week. It does not matter what the job is, it does not matter what the
impact is, it does not matter whether there is adequate childcare, and so on. So I say to
members opposite that if they are going to bring in this policy, then where is the plan to
make it work? It is not in the legislation; it is not in anything that the Minister has said
to date about how these people will be assisted into jobs, when the jobs come.
I bring the Committee’s attention to a number of amendments that Labour has put
forward on this bill. I say to the Minister that if she is going to bring in this policy, why
does she not change the 15 hours of work a week to 20 hours before the part-time work
test is applied? Just a few moments ago the Minister, in her own speech, said that the
reason sole parents went off the sole parent benefit was Working for Families. Does the
Minister recall that? That is what she said. She said that sole parents went off the benefit
because of Working for Families. What does Working for Families provide? It provides
17 Aug 2010 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 13185
that those people who undertake 20 hours of part-time work a week are eligible for the
in-work tax credit. Why does the Minister not make the part-time work test apply at 20
hours of work a week? If that does what the Minister said it does, why not apply the 20
hours rather than the 15 hours? I urge the Māori Party, the ACT Party—

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.role: Minister for Social Development and Employment
items.text: I
will note a couple of quick things, particularly in relation to the Green member’s
contribution about advance payments and hardship in clause 23. In the election
manifesto we came into Government on we said we were going to have compulsory
budgeting for those who had had, I think, two or more advance payments. We looked at
that with the benefit of hindsight, and we saw that it was not realistic.
I acknowledge what the Green member was saying, in that actually we look at
them—

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What if they don’t have the money?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I was trying to address what the member had said and
was giving another perspective. What we were trying to do with clause 23, and what we
have done, is say that it is a budgeting activity. It might be more that people are sitting
down with their case managers and working out what is working for them. I also
thought that process might actually help them to make sure they are getting all of their
entitlements. We are making sure they are getting everything.
The other thing that we are doing with the budgeting activity is taking account of the
things that are available via the Internet. One just needs to look at the Sorted website
and those sorts of sites to see that they can provide opportunities for people. We also
want to look at what we can do to assist people when they get further down the track, so
there is budgeting assistance for them there.
In recognition of the honourable member who has just spoken, Mrs King, I will
address the issue of 15 or 20 hours of work. The official part-time figure is 15 hours;
that is where that figure came from. It is a minimum. I could not agree more that the
jump for an extra 5 hours makes an incredible difference for those who are on the
domestic purposes benefit, but 15 hours is the official part-time figure. That is why it
was chosen. It also fits in with some of the hours that they can get with jobs—for
example, 2 full-time days of 7 hours. It recognises some of those differences, and 15
hours is a minimum. We certainly see the financial benefits of those on benefits going
into 20 hours’ work. I have no hesitation in recommending that.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The Minister for Social
Development and Employment can, at this stage, change the minimum hours to 20, and
I suggest that the Minister does that. There is nothing magical about 15 hours, either. I
say she should make it 20 hours. The Minister could put forward an amendment to the
Social Assistance (New Work Tests, Incentives, and Obligations) Amendment Bill; she
is in charge of her own legislation.
The next thing I say to the Minister is that when the issue of the abatement level was
brought up at the Social Services Committee—and her members on that committee
would have told the Minister this—it was told that lifting the abatement level from $80
a week to $100 a week does not take account of the increase that there has been through
the CPI over the years since the level was last changed. Some people have said the
abatement level should be $160 a week, but the consensus at the select committee was
that it should be $130 a week. Why does the Minister not increase it to $130 a week? I
see she has had the Minister of Finance put a financial veto on that, but that would be
the fair thing to do.
The next issue is the commencement date of 27 September, I believe. Why does the
Minister not extend the commencement date out, to line it up with the Government’s
own unemployment benefit predictions? We have talked a lot tonight about the fact that
13186 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 17 Aug 2010
there are not a lot of jobs out there for people around New Zealand. There are not a lot
of jobs, particularly in the provinces and in some of the smaller places in New Zealand.
The Minister would have heard from Shane Jones about unemployment in the far north,
where it is almost in double figures. So why does the Minister not extend the
commencement date out, to line it up with the unemployment beneficiary predictions
that are in the Budget documents this year? Those Budget documents show that the
number of people on the unemployment benefit will still be higher in 2014 than it was
when the Minister took office. It will be higher in 2014 than it was when we left
Government. So there will be a large number of people on the unemployment benefit
who want to obtain jobs, in a market where there will still be few jobs. Even if the
Minister does not want to go as far as doing that, why does she not push out the date at
which the Government will bring this legislation into force? I think the Government will
start to look very silly when it does not achieve what it says this legislation will achieve.
I also would like the Minister to consider the submission that asked her to please
look at the evidence. She was asked to look at the evidence of what works and what
does not work. One of the pieces of information that came from Massey University was
that change comes from the availability of work, not from sanctions. So the availability
of work for beneficiaries has to be the prerequisite to get them into work, rather than
sanctions.
My last comment is that I believe that most beneficiaries in New Zealand want to
have a job. That has been shown. Did people see the woman tonight, on television, who
has just got a job at the supermarket in Mount Roskill? She has been trying to get a job
for 2 long years—

items.speaker: H V Ross Robertson
items.text: 2,500 applied!

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: —and 2,700 people lined up to work in the supermarket.
She got one of the jobs, and the smile on her face was huge, because she wanted to have
a job. She wanted to work; she did not want to be on a benefit. She, in my view, reflects
the view of many people around New Zealand who want to have a job.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: So she was made unemployed under Labour.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: She may well have become unemployed when we were in
Government, I tell Dr Smith, but when we left Government, New Zealand had the
lowest unemployment rate in the Western World. It is now, under this Government,
going up every month. So I would not harp on about that, if I were Dr Smith. It will be
another bit of misinformation that he provides to the House. That woman got a job.
Most beneficiaries want to have a job, but this legislation will not make a single job
available for them.
I say the Minister should base her legislation on evidence. I also say the Minister has
not provided any evidence that this legislation will work. The Government has been told
that over and over again. The Government’s own regulatory impact statement stated that
there is no evidence of that, and its own Attorney-General, who is its top legal person,
has said this legislation is discriminatory.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: Just to follow on from my earlier
discussion about the advance payment of benefits, the Minister in the chair, the Hon
Paula Bennett, stood up to say that people can do a budgeting activity—which is not
very different from budgeting advice or trying to organise for beneficiaries to rearrange
their money better—knowing, as she does, full well that there simply is not enough
money, and that beneficiaries seek support through advances in various forms because
they do not have enough money to cover the very basics. Of course, we saw an example
of exactly that today in the newspaper. Although the Minister will spin this measure as
being one to try to help beneficiaries, at the root of what she is says, and at the root of
the provision in clause 23 of the Social Assistance (New Work Tests, Incentives, and
17 Aug 2010 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 13187
Obligations) Amendment Bill is the assumption that if beneficiaries cannot manage on
an income that is insufficient, that must be entirely their fault. It is assumed that they
must obviously be people who are not doing a good enough job of managing on money
that simply cannot be stretched any further to cover the very basics.
The Minister herself would understand what that means, having been in a similar
situation to that previously, as do I and as do others in this Chamber who have been in
similar situations. We understand what it means to not have enough money to cover the
very basics, and to need help. In the current situation, with the regulated temporary
additional support, we now have very set criteria that do not take into account the
circumstances of a particular parent and what he or she needs. It might be the case that
his or her child has over the last few weeks been extremely ill, so the parent has had real
difficulty in going to a part-time job, which maybe brings in 50 or 80 bucks a week so
the parent does not lose money on the abatement. There might be very basic, particular
circumstances, but if people fail the regulatory tests set out in the legislation, then they
will not be able to access that additional support. They will go without the very basics,
and so will their children.
The other part of this measure is weird, in the sense that it talks about an excessive
number of advance payments. It says those who seek an excessive number of advance
payments will have to seek budgetary advice. Again, that goes directly to the blame-the-
victim mentality that is part of this legislation.
We need to provide in welfare legislation systems that are simple, understandable,
and transparent; that incentivise beneficiaries to gain the extra skills that they need in
order to move into the workforce when they are ready; and that provide support for the
children of beneficiaries to be parented as effectively as possible. When a sole parent is
on the domestic purposes benefit, we have a real opportunity for skill development. If
the person does not have a very good education or has not had an opportunity to get
further development or training, we should look at their skills and support them to train
for better skills. There is an opportunity to support sole parents to get access to child
care, so that their children get very good high-quality early childhood education, which
they can participate in and be part of. There are a lot of excellent opportunities in early
childhood education for parents to be involved with their children on a regular daily
basis, without the stress of having to find work or of being forced to lose their benefit as
a result of not finding the work that their case manager says they should find.
There are ways to give families the support that they need in order to do the best job
of taking care of their babies and children. But what happens with legislation like this—
which is based on a blame-the-victim mentality and a punitive approach, whereby
people whose circumstances mean that they need help now are punished for needing
that help—is that at the end of the day it punishes the children of those families.
I support the amendments that the Hon Annette King has put forward. I agree
entirely with her comments on the 20 hours a week. The Government, by making the
work test 15 hours a week and not 20 hours a week, is cutting off for beneficiaries the
opportunity to make the step up from the benefit. It constrains their ability to move off
the benefit and into 20-hour work, where they could then move into being supported by
Working for Families. It traps beneficiaries into the poverty cycle. The idea that there
are a whole lot of 2-day-a-week, 7-hour-a-day jobs is just unrealistic and untrue.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: I rise to agree with other colleagues about our
fundamental concern regarding the provisions of the Social Assistance (New Work
Tests, Incentives, and Obligations) Amendment Bill, and particularly about the
provisions in it around work testing and the discriminatory nature of the bill. I think the
really concerning thing is the statement in the commentary on the bill about the
unrelenting focus on work. It is as though if we say something often enough, that makes
13188 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 17 Aug 2010
it true. That seems to be the approach of this Government. It thinks that if it says the
word “productivity” often enough, then people will believe it is doing something about
productivity. It thinks that if it says it has an unrelenting focus on work, then maybe
people will believe that it does have an unrelenting focus on work.
The reality is that, in substantial part, this bill is nothing less than an attack on
beneficiaries, and a discriminatory one at that. It is unfair. The Attorney-General has
judged the bill to be discriminatory. It certainly does not focus on work. This bill does
not create any jobs. As the Minister for Social Development and Employment, Paula
Bennett, said, it is really about giving a kick in the pants to beneficiaries. The regulatory
impact statement said there is no available research that accurately quantifies the size of
the behavioural response to these changes in policy. In other words, this is about politics
rather than practical work. It is about the Government liking to use the old dog whistle,
as one of my colleagues said previously. There are a few dog whistles that it likes to roll
out now and then, and beneficiary bashing is one of them. There was no consultation
with beneficiary groups before this bill was introduced. Virtually all of the Government
departments that were consulted over this bill had concerns about it. It certainly seems
that all of the submitters, or the overwhelming majority of them, believed that this bill is
about beneficiary bashing.
I say that what really needs to happen is for the Government to focus on creating
jobs. There are 159,000 people who are out of work. We all know that the best way to
get people off benefits is to have jobs for them to go to. That is simple. If we look at the
number of jobs available, we find that benefit numbers fall when job numbers increase.
It really is quite remarkable that the Minister actually acknowledged that changes like
those in this legislation should not be implemented when there is no labour-market
recovery. She said that herself. Perhaps this legislation needs to be delayed now, in light
of the most recent unemployment figures. The unemployment rate has gone up from 6
percent to 6.8 percent in the June quarter. Perhaps we should look at some of those
figures a little more. That is 159,000 people—up by 19,000 over the last 3 months. That
is above the number that Treasury had predicted. Since this Government has been in
office, unemployment has increased by 53,000 people. What is the Government doing
to create jobs? What is it doing to adjust the economic fundamentals that provide the
macroeconomic policy settings for the creation of jobs? Nothing; there is no plan.
Let me take the time to talk about just one particular area, which is skills
development. In this country it is absolutely shocking that in a time of high
unemployment we are not investing more in upskilling our workforce and dealing with
some of the fundamental gaps that we have in our labour force. I had a woman come
into my office the other day. She had been made redundant after she had worked in a
job for 30 years. She had no idea about job hunting, and furthermore her skills were
very narrowly focused towards the job that she had been doing for the last 30 years. I do
not think that that is amusing. There was no opportunity for her to change that situation.
She wanted to have a job, and she would have put effort into trying to change her
situation. But, of course, adult and community education has been fundamentally
destroyed by this Government, and furthermore there is no real focus on providing
opportunities to upskill our existing workforce. Attention is being paid only to pre-entry
training, and even there we find really significant limits. There are limits on access to
tertiary education, for example.
If we look at skills development for the existing workforce, what do we see in this
Budget? I tell people that we see absolutely nothing. This year’s Budget had no new
initiatives in that area. We saw Department of Labour funding going from the skills area
to the area of hazardous substances and new organisms. The hazardous substances and
17 Aug 2010 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 13189
new organisms area is important, but skills development, in an economic recession like
the one that we have now, is far more important.

items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Chairperson. I am sorry, Mr Chairperson, but I think I have recorded most of the Māori

votes, and I offer my apologies to the Minister. If there were to be a blanket change to
all of our votes, one of the five votes that I registered would be put on the other side of

with the Opposition?

17 Aug 2010 Speaker’s Statements 13107 
TUESDAY, 17 AUGUST 2010 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
SPEAKER’S STATEMENTS 
Hon Chris Carter—Change of Parliamentary Membership 
Mr SPEAKER: Under Standing Order 35(1)(c) I have been advised by the Labour 
Party that its parliamentary membership has changed, and that the Hon Chris Carter is 
no longer a member of the Labour Party for parliamentary purposes. Accordingly, under 
Standing Order 34(4) the Hon Chris Carter is from 10 August 2010 regarded as an 
Independent member for parliamentary purposes. Allocations of speaking slots and oral 
questions have been adjusted. Allocations of funding to the Labour Party and to the Hon 
Chris Carter have also been adjusted.  
POINTS OF ORDER 
Land Transport (Safer Alcohol Limits for Driving) Amendment Bill—Leave to 
Introduce 
Hon DARREN HUGHES (Senior Whip—Labour): I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. As advised to parties this morning, I seek leave for the Land Transport (Safer 
Alcohol Limits for Driving) Amendment Bill to be introduced and set down as a 
members’ order of the day.  
Mr SPEAKER: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection? 
There is objection.  
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Recession—Prime Minister’s Statements 
1. Hon PHIL GOFF (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement that by March 2010 New Zealand will be coming out of the

Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister for Social Development and Employment): I 
stand in response to some of the rather emotive debate that has gone on around this bill 
so far. First, I say that 28,000 people on the benefit will be better off because of this bill, 
pretty much immediately, and that is because of the abatement increase from $80 to 
$100 per week that they can earn. This is a very good day for those people in that they 
will be recognised for the work they do and they are able to get more of that money in 
their own pocket and see it as the opportunity that it is. 
This is a bill that recognises fairness, that brings equity back into the system, and that 
steps up in support of those people who, quite frankly, deserve our support and need it 
most. The bill injects a whole lot around them and gives them the opportunity to take up 
the training opportunities they need, and it provides support around them so that they 
have the opportunity to look for work. I think it will put the right incentives in place 
and, with that, the right sorts of obligations. 
There are exemptions in relation to those things, and I heard through the Social 
Services Committee that there were concerns about those people who perhaps had 
recently left a relationship and were going through some of the emotional trauma that 
that can cause. There is an exemption to enable those people to take time and to 
recognise what that means. There is an exemption in recognition of those who have 
perhaps come from a violent background and need time to bed in with their children. 
There are exemptions for those who have children with special needs who perhaps need 
their parents a bit more. So there are exemptions there for them. 
There is also a clear understanding of what suitable work means. The bill recognises 
that childcare is needed for those children and that what is needed is the opportunity for 
people to have work that fits in with the hours that they need, that they are able to get to 
the jobs as they come up, and that they have the sort of lines they need so that they can 
get to them. It is very important that they have that. 
I heard members opposite asking what the definition of suitable work is. Let me give 
it to them to clear that up. It is that there is an availability of childcare; that it is not 
employment with excessive hours; that their case managers recognise family 
commitments and religious commitments, which are important for some of those 
people; and that they are not jobs that offend strongly held views. There are regulations 
around that, as well. The days of the week, the type of employment, and the skills and 
experience required are all important justifications to make sure that that job suits the 
individual. I suppose that is what I wanted to say. 
The thing I will also add here is that there are no penalties for not getting work. I will 
repeat that one more time because it is really important: there are no penalties, 
whatsoever, for not getting work. The only penalties there are for people who are not 
actually trying. So we are asking people to get themselves work-ready—to be going out 
and looking for work, and to be actively looking to support themselves and their own. 
Among those on the sickness benefit, 9,000 currently have a box ticked by their doctors

want to clarify a few things because I think that anyone listening in just then might have

be made if they are stepping up and looking for work. So I just clarify that. The likeness 
to the US was completely misleading. We are talking about part-time work-testing for 
those who can find a job when their youngest child is 6. I want to be clear about that 
sort of thing.

the number of beneficiaries will go down, and it will be fine and everything else.

in those best of times. We saw a very limited reduction in the number on the domestic 
purposes benefit, but that was more as a result of Working for Families, when we saw a 
few thousand people move off the domestic purposes benefit as that was more 
accessible for them.

an increase of 45 percent in the number of people on the sickness benefit. At a time 
when New Zealanders are not becoming more sick, when they are starting to live

Maharey in the last Labour Government. Minister Maharey abolished the special

removed a level of discretion from the third-tier welfare assistance programme. What 
this Government does not understand, and what was unfortunate about Minister

have ordinary lives that they have to live and simply do not have the income to pay the

absolutely desperate when they come in for temporary additional support. But when we 
take that away, people fall through the cracks. Those people are desperately in need of a

she was a Minister of the Crown in the New Zealand Parliament and should be 
applauded for that. So I say to the Minister that she brought herself into the debate, and 
if it is mentioned by members on this side of the Chamber, then it is because we see it 
as an OK thing to do because she did it. Other members, including me, have tonight 
talked about their experiences. 
Tau Henare said that the Minister came from the school of hard knocks. But I have to 
say that she also came from a university education, and we have been saying to 
members opposite that if this bill is going to do what National claims, then where is the 
plan to get people into work? I want to go into that issue in a moment. 
First of all, I want to answer some points made by Hekia Parata. She said in her 
speech that there needs to be reciprocity. When the Crown is providing assistance to 
those who are on a benefit, then there is some obligation on their part, and I agree with 
her. But I ask that member what is magical about the youngest child being 6. I had one 
child, and it was a lot easier to be able to do other things when she was 6. But if I had 
been a sole parent and had had a 6-year-old, a 7-year-old, a 9-year-old, and an 11-year-
old, the situation would have been totally different. Setting a policy around the youngest 
child being 6 does not take account of the other circumstances within that family 
situation. That is why it was said in submissions—which the member would have 
heard—that if we were to use the policy that exists now within the Ministry of Social 
Development, we would have the flexibility to do exactly what this Government wants 
to do without actually bringing in legislation. 
Members on this side of the Chamber believe that every New Zealander should have 
the chance of the Kiwi dream of having a decent job. We want New Zealanders to have 
a decent job, with decent pay. But how do we put a person who is on a benefit on that 
path? We do not do it by telling them that they have to be work tested when their 
youngest child is 6, regardless of the circumstances, and that they need to be able to do 
15 hours of work a week. It does not matter what the job is, it does not matter what the 
impact is, it does not matter whether there is adequate childcare, and so on. So I say to 
members opposite that if they are going to bring in this policy, then where is the plan to 
make it work? It is not in the legislation; it is not in anything that the Minister has said 
to date about how these people will be assisted into jobs, when the jobs come. 
I bring the Committee’s attention to a number of amendments that Labour has put 
forward on this bill. I say to the Minister that if she is going to bring in this policy, why 
does she not change the 15 hours of work a week to 20 hours before the part-time work

because of Working for Families. What does Working for Families provide? It provides

Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister for Social Development and Employment): I

domestic purposes benefit, but 15 hours is the official part-time figure. That is why it 
was chosen. It also fits in with some of the hours that they can get with jobs—for 
example, 2 full-time days of 7 hours. It recognises some of those differences, and 15 
hours is a minimum. We certainly see the financial benefits of those on benefits going 
into 20 hours’ work. I have no hesitation in recommending that.  
Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader—Labour): The Minister for Social 
Development and Employment can, at this stage, change the minimum hours to 20, and 
I suggest that the Minister does that. There is nothing magical about 15 hours, either. I 
say she should make it 20 hours. The Minister could put forward an amendment to the 
Social Assistance (New Work Tests, Incentives, and Obligations) Amendment Bill; she 
is in charge of her own legislation.  
The next thing I say to the Minister is that when the issue of the abatement level was

would have told the Minister this—it was told that lifting the abatement level from $80 
a week to $100 a week does not take account of the increase that there has been through 
the CPI over the years since the level was last changed. Some people have said the 
abatement level should be $160 a week, but the consensus at the select committee was 
that it should be $130 a week. Why does the Minister not increase it to $130 a week? I 
see she has had the Minister of Finance put a financial veto on that, but that would be 
the fair thing to do.  
The next issue is the commencement date of 27 September, I believe. Why does the

own unemployment benefit predictions? We have talked a lot tonight about the fact that 
13186 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 17 Aug 2010 
there are not a lot of jobs out there for people around New Zealand. There are not a lot 
of jobs, particularly in the provinces and in some of the smaller places in New Zealand. 
The Minister would have heard from Shane Jones about unemployment in the far north,

commencement date out, to line it up with the unemployment beneficiary predictions

who want to obtain jobs, in a market where there will still be few jobs. Even if the 
Minister does not want to go as far as doing that, why does she not push out the date at

start to look very silly when it does not achieve what it says this legislation will achieve.  
I also would like the Minister to consider the submission that asked her to please 
look at the evidence. She was asked to look at the evidence of what works and what

that change comes from the availability of work, not from sanctions. So the availability 
of work for beneficiaries has to be the prerequisite to get them into work, rather than 
sanctions.  
My last comment is that I believe that most beneficiaries in New Zealand want to 
have a job. That has been shown. Did people see the woman tonight, on television, who 
has just got a job at the supermarket in Mount Roskill? She has been trying to get a job 
for 2 long years— 
H V Ross Robertson: 2,500 applied! 
Hon ANNETTE KING: —and 2,700 people lined up to work in the supermarket. 
She got one of the jobs, and the smile on her face was huge, because she wanted to have 
a job. She wanted to work; she did not want to be on a benefit. She, in my view, reflects 
the view of many people around New Zealand who want to have a job.  
Hon Dr Nick Smith: So she was made unemployed under Labour. 
Hon ANNETTE KING: She may well have become unemployed when we were in 
Government, I tell Dr Smith, but when we left Government, New Zealand had the 
lowest unemployment rate in the Western World. It is now, under this Government, 
going up every month. So I would not harp on about that, if I were Dr Smith. It will be 
another bit of misinformation that he provides to the House. That woman got a job. 
Most beneficiaries want to have a job, but this legislation will not make a single job 
available for them.  
I say the Minister should base her legislation on evidence. I also say the Minister has 
not provided any evidence that this legislation will work. The Government has been told 
that over and over again. The Government’s own regulatory impact statement stated that 
there is no evidence of that, and its own Attorney-General, who is its top legal person, 
has said this legislation is discriminatory.  
METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green): Just to follow on from my earlier 
discussion about the advance payment of benefits, the Minister in the chair, the Hon 
Paula Bennett, stood up to say that people can do a budgeting activity—which is not 
very different from budgeting advice or trying to organise for beneficiaries to rearrange 
their money better—knowing, as she does, full well that there simply is not enough 
money, and that beneficiaries seek support through advances in various forms because 
they do not have enough money to cover the very basics. Of course, we saw an example 
of exactly that today in the newspaper. Although the Minister will spin this measure as 
being one to try to help beneficiaries, at the root of what she is says, and at the root of 
the provision in clause 23 of the Social Assistance (New Work Tests, Incentives, and 
17 Aug 2010 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 13187 
Obligations) Amendment Bill is the assumption that if beneficiaries cannot manage on 
an income that is insufficient, that must be entirely their fault. It is assumed that they 
must obviously be people who are not doing a good enough job of managing on money 
that simply cannot be stretched any further to cover the very basics.  
The Minister herself would understand what that means, having been in a similar 
situation to that previously, as do I and as do others in this Chamber who have been in 
similar situations. We understand what it means to not have enough money to cover the 
very basics, and to need help. In the current situation, with the regulated temporary 
additional support, we now have very set criteria that do not take into account the 
circumstances of a particular parent and what he or she needs. It might be the case that 
his or her child has over the last few weeks been extremely ill, so the parent has had real 
difficulty in going to a part-time job, which maybe brings in 50 or 80 bucks a week so 
the parent does not lose money on the abatement. There might be very basic, particular 
circumstances, but if people fail the regulatory tests set out in the legislation, then they 
will not be able to access that additional support. They will go without the very basics, 
and so will their children.  
The other part of this measure is weird, in the sense that it talks about an excessive 
number of advance payments. It says those who seek an excessive number of advance 
payments will have to seek budgetary advice. Again, that goes directly to the blame-the-
victim mentality that is part of this legislation.  
We need to provide in welfare legislation systems that are simple, understandable, 
and transparent; that incentivise beneficiaries to gain the extra skills that they need in 
order to move into the workforce when they are ready; and that provide support for the 
children of beneficiaries to be parented as effectively as possible. When a sole parent is 
on the domestic purposes benefit, we have a real opportunity for skill development. If 
the person does not have a very good education or has not had an opportunity to get 
further development or training, we should look at their skills and support them to train 
for better skills. There is an opportunity to support sole parents to get access to child 
care, so that their children get very good high-quality early childhood education, which 
they can participate in and be part of. There are a lot of excellent opportunities in early 
childhood education for parents to be involved with their children on a regular daily 
basis, without the stress of having to find work or of being forced to lose their benefit as 
a result of not finding the work that their case manager says they should find.  
There are ways to give families the support that they need in order to do the best job 
of taking care of their babies and children. But what happens with legislation like this—
which is based on a blame-the-victim mentality and a punitive approach, whereby 
people whose circumstances mean that they need help now are punished for needing 
that help—is that at the end of the day it punishes the children of those families.  
I support the amendments that the Hon Annette King has put forward. I agree 
entirely with her comments on the 20 hours a week. The Government, by making the 
work test 15 hours a week and not 20 hours a week, is cutting off for beneficiaries the 
opportunity to make the step up from the benefit. It constrains their ability to move off 
the benefit and into 20-hour work, where they could then move into being supported by 
Working for Families. It traps beneficiaries into the poverty cycle. The idea that there 
are a whole lot of 2-day-a-week, 7-hour-a-day jobs is just unrealistic and untrue. 
CAROL BEAUMONT (Labour): I rise to agree with other colleagues about our 
fundamental concern regarding the provisions of the Social Assistance (New Work 
Tests, Incentives, and Obligations) Amendment Bill, and particularly about the 
provisions in it around work testing and the discriminatory nature of the bill. I think the 
really concerning thing is the statement in the commentary on the bill about the 
unrelenting focus on work. It is as though if we say something often enough, that makes 
13188 Social Assistance (Work Tests etc.) Amdt Bill 17 Aug 2010 
it true. That seems to be the approach of this Government. It thinks that if it says the 
word “productivity” often enough, then people will believe it is doing something about 
productivity. It thinks that if it says it has an unrelenting focus on work, then maybe 
people will believe that it does have an unrelenting focus on work.  
The reality is that, in substantial part, this bill is nothing less than an attack on 
beneficiaries, and a discriminatory one at that. It is unfair. The Attorney-General has 
judged the bill to be discriminatory. It certainly does not focus on work. This bill does 
not create any jobs. As the Minister for Social Development and Employment, Paula 
Bennett, said, it is really about giving a kick in the pants to beneficiaries. The regulatory 
impact statement said there is no available research that accurately quantifies the size of 
the behavioural response to these changes in policy. In other words, this is about politics 
rather than practical work. It is about the Government liking to use the old dog whistle, 
as one of my colleagues said previously. There are a few dog whistles that it likes to roll 
out now and then, and beneficiary bashing is one of them. There was no consultation 
with beneficiary groups before this bill was introduced. Virtually all of the Government 
departments that were consulted over this bill had concerns about it. It certainly seems 
that all of the submitters, or the overwhelming majority of them, believed that this bill is 
about beneficiary bashing.  
I say that what really needs to happen is for the Government to focus on creating 
jobs. There are 159,000 people who are out of work. We all know that the best way to 
get people off benefits is to have jobs for them to go to. That is simple. If we look at the 
number of jobs available, we find that benefit numbers fall when job numbers increase. 
It really is quite remarkable that the Minister actually acknowledged that changes like 
those in this legislation should not be implemented when there is no labour-market 
recovery. She said that herself. Perhaps this legislation needs to be delayed now, in light 
of the most recent unemployment figures. The unemployment rate has gone up from 6 
percent to 6.8 percent in the June quarter. Perhaps we should look at some of those 
figures a little more. That is 159,000 people—up by 19,000 over the last 3 months. That 
is above the number that Treasury had predicted. Since this Government has been in 
office, unemployment has increased by 53,000 people. What is the Government doing 
to create jobs? What is it doing to adjust the economic fundamentals that provide the 
macroeconomic policy settings for the creation of jobs? Nothing; there is no plan.  
Let me take the time to talk about just one particular area, which is skills 
development. In this country it is absolutely shocking that in a time of high 
unemployment we are not investing more in upskilling our workforce and dealing with 
some of the fundamental gaps that we have in our labour force. I had a woman come 
into my office the other day. She had been made redundant after she had worked in a 
job for 30 years. She had no idea about job hunting, and furthermore her skills were 
very narrowly focused towards the job that she had been doing for the last 30 years. I do 
not think that that is amusing. There was no opportunity for her to change that situation. 
She wanted to have a job, and she would have put effort into trying to change her 
situation. But, of course, adult and community education has been fundamentally 
destroyed by this Government, and furthermore there is no real focus on providing 
opportunities to upskill our existing workforce. Attention is being paid only to pre-entry 
training, and even there we find really significant limits. There are limits on access to 
tertiary education, for example.  
If we look at skills development for the existing workforce, what do we see in this 
Budget? I tell people that we see absolutely nothing. This year’s Budget had no new 
initiatives in that area. We saw Department of Labour funding going from the skills area 
to the area of hazardous substances and new organisms. The hazardous substances and

the one that we have now, is far more important.
